stories.headline: A backdoored build of the official Claude Code extension hit the Cursor Marketplace
stories.why_read: You live in Cursor and Claude Code every day, so check your extension version before you do anything else this morning.
body: Security firm Phorion says it found a backdoor in the official Claude Code for VS Code extension bundle served by the Cursor Marketplace. The tainted version, 2.1.313, drops a persistent SSH backdoor and includes setup and persistence logic for macOS, Linux, and Windows. Phorion says Cursor has removed the release from its marketplace, and that the 2.1.313 builds were also pulled from npm and the VS Code registry.

Phorion's advice is blunt: look for Claude Code for VS Code 2.1.313 anywhere in your environment and bring in incident response if you find it, because an extension runs with the full permissions of the editor and the user. Kevin Beaumont flagged it on Mastodon this morning, and DoublePulsar's write-up framed it as Anthropic itself being compromised. The story is only hours old, so expect details on how the build was tampered with to keep changing.

stories.headline: Tesla makes your first Robotaxi ride free in Houston and Dallas as Cybercabs overtake Model Ys in Texas
stories.why_read: You bookmarked AIDRIVR's "first one's on me" joke about this; here's the promotion and the fleet numbers behind it.
body: Tesla is offering free first rides on its Robotaxi service in Houston and Dallas, according to X's news summary, with riders posting screenshots of late-night pickups. It lands as the Texas fleet keeps growing: the summary puts Cybercab registrations at 573, ahead of 507 Model Ys, for about 1,080 vehicles, with recent additions all Cybercabs.

Houston riders describe trips under 15 minutes and clean handling in tight spots and near construction, though the service still avoids highways. Dallas rides are slated for next month. AIDRIVR summed up the promotion with "'First one's on me' said the drug dealer," which is about as honest a description of a customer-acquisition offer as you'll find.

stories.headline: Mistral releases the weights of Mistral Large 4, a 1-trillion-parameter open model
stories.why_read: A frontier-scale open-weight model aimed squarely at agentic coding, which is exactly the open-source LLM beat you follow.
body: Mistral has released the weights of Mistral Large 4, nicknamed Le Chonk, a natively multimodal model with 1 trillion parameters that entered public preview earlier this month. Mistral says three more weeks of reinforcement learning since the preview pushed it to the front of open-weight coding: it scores 19.7 percent on Cognition's private FrontierCode 2.0 benchmark and 41 percent on Terminal-Bench 4.0, up 13 points from the preview.

On the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index it scores 48 percent, effectively tied with GLM-5.3 while using 47 percent fewer tokens per task, and it now offers three reasoning modes to trade cost against depth. Mistral pitches it as a sovereign-AI option trained from scratch on European infrastructure. It was one of the top stories on Hacker News overnight with more than 1,500 points.

stories.headline: Binance loses more than $6 billion in the largest crypto theft on record
stories.why_read: A reminder that one compromised engineer laptop can be a multibillion-dollar incident, which is worth sitting with next to today's lead.
body: Binance froze withdrawals after digital assets worth more than $6.3 billion were taken, according to The Guardian's live coverage, apparently after a laptop belonging to one of its engineers was hacked. Blockchain intelligence firm TRM attributes the theft to North Korea's TraderTraitor unit, and Chainalysis says the hackers are using laundering patterns it hasn't seen before.

Binance says user funds are safe and that it has located about $3 billion of the assets with partners, while co-founder Yi He said the company would cover all hacking losses. UK financial watchdogs say they are monitoring the fallout. The Hacker News thread passed 1,400 points.

stories.headline: Patrick Stewart has died
stories.why_read: You reposted Hugh Jackman's tribute last night; it was the highest-scoring story on today's Hacker News front page.
body: Patrick Stewart, the stage and screen actor beloved as Star Trek's Captain Jean-Luc Picard and X-Men's Professor Charles Xavier, has died, The New York Times reported. The news drew more than 3,000 points on Hacker News, a measure of how much Picard meant to engineers.

Hugh Jackman, his X-Men co-star, wrote: "We lost one of the greats of stage and screen today. And, in my book, a tremendous friend and man. I learned so much from him. I will miss you, Patrick Stewart, all of my days."

stories.headline: Musk shares progress on Terafab, the Tesla and SpaceX chip factory going up near Houston
stories.why_read: A Texas-built chip fab for Tesla and SpaceX AI hardware sits right where your chips and Tesla interests meet.
body: Elon Musk posted progress on Terafab, the chip factory Tesla and SpaceX are building in Grimes County near Houston, with a research site near Austin. According to X's news summary, the plan covers design, fabrication, packaging, and testing in one complex, at a reported cost of $16.8 billion, with volume production targeted for the third quarter of 2028.

What people are talking about most is the pace: suppliers answering in under an hour and engineers making calls on the spot. Skeptics still question whether a brand-new fab can hold that speed, but the project fits the broader push for U.S. chip supply for AI and robotics.

stories.headline: SpaceX starts winding down Falcon 9 and Crew Dragon government work to focus on Starship
stories.why_read: A big strategic turn for the company you follow most closely, with real consequences for NASA.
body: SpaceX has told NASA it plans to retire Crew Dragon operations by 2030, has stopped taking new commercial Falcon 9 sales after 2028, and has declined bids from the U.S. Space Force and NASA's lunar payload program, according to X's news summary of the reports. It will honor existing commitments while it redirects effort to Starship, Starlink, and its AI business.

Observers see it as a sign of independence that opens room for Blue Origin and others, but it raises questions about NASA's Artemis timeline and how crews get to the ISS. It pairs with a separate debate, started by Ars Technica's Eric Berger, about whether Starship needs a traditional payload door before it can truly replace Falcon 9 for big satellites and station modules.

stories.headline: Grace Blackwell racks need a new kind of scheduler, and getting it right frees up 27% more GPUs
stories.why_read: Practical systems thinking about NVL72 racks, the kind of infrastructure detail an architect actually uses.
body: SkyPilot argues that Nvidia's NVL72 systems, which join all 72 GPUs in a rack into one NVLink fabric, change how clusters should be scheduled. Running the same distributed training job over InfiniBand instead of NVLink can cut performance by 43 percent, so a multi-node job that spills across racks loses much of the benefit.

The post walks through why rack-locality gets harder as hardware failures take nodes offline and jobs finish at different times, and how topology-aware placement, in-place recovery, and automatic defragmentation keep jobs inside a rack. SkyPilot says the approach yields about 27 percent more usable GPUs from the same racks.

stories.headline: SpaceX filings name Anthropic as its biggest customer, at 34.5% of third-quarter revenue
stories.why_read: The AI compute story and the SpaceX story turn out to be the same story.
body: SpaceX's filings identify Anthropic as "Customer B," responsible for 34.5 percent of third-quarter revenue through compute from SpaceX's Memphis facilities, ahead of NASA and the Pentagon, according to X's news summary. The commitments run up to $120.5 billion through 2029.

The disclosure lands just after Anthropic filed for its Nasdaq IPO under the ticker ANT, per the same summary, and it raises the obvious question of customer concentration for SpaceX. In the bookmarks you saved, Sam Parr estimated that about 1,000 Anthropic employees could be worth more than $100 million each at a $2 trillion valuation.

stories.headline: Nvidia weighs billions in credit guarantees for an Nscale data center that would run Anthropic on Vera Rubin
stories.why_read: Nvidia is now underwriting the buildings its chips go into, which says a lot about how this buildout is being financed.
body: Nvidia is in talks to back a 460-megawatt facility at Nscale's Monarch campus in West Virginia, where Anthropic plans to run compute on Nvidia's upcoming Vera Rubin GPUs as part of a $45 billion cloud deal, according to X's news summary. The proposed support, estimated at more than $5 billion, would cover power infrastructure and construction through a residual value guarantee.

If Nscale defaulted, Nvidia could step in to cover payments and arrange a sale or re-lease. The deal isn't signed and terms could change, but it fits Nvidia's pattern of helping to create demand for its own chips.

stories.headline: Google Cloud growth hits 103% as all three hyperscalers accelerate
stories.why_read: You reposted this chart last night, and the AWS number you bookmarked puts the scale in perspective.
body: A chart you reposted from @MinuteMoola tracks the last four quarters of cloud growth: AWS went from 24 to 28 to 37 to 39 percent, Google Cloud from 48 to 63 to 82 to 103 percent, and Azure from 39 to 40 to 40 to 48 percent. The post's conclusion: "This isn't what AI slowing down looks like, this is AI speeding up."
For scale, Jon Erlichman noted in a post you bookmarked that AWS brought in $21 million in revenue in all of 2006 and now brings in $21 million every hour.

stories.headline: CI Playbooks: 253 GitHub Actions speedups collected from teams running software factories
stories.why_read: As agents write more of the code, CI becomes the bottleneck; this is a concrete list of fixes you can hand to an agent.
body: @yonasbe introduced CI Playbooks, a library of 253 GitHub Actions optimizations distilled from 416 pull requests and commits and 182 blog posts, talks, and podcasts from ten companies. The examples are striking: Anthropic's CI job volume grew 25x in six months as Claude came to write 80 percent of its code, DoorDash cut build and test from 22 minutes to 6, and Ramp's coding agent now accounts for 74 percent of merged PRs.

Where companies don't use GitHub Actions internally, the techniques were translated into GitHub Actions equivalents. Every playbook links its original source and ships with a prompt your coding agent can run against your repo.

stories.headline: Thorsten Ball: you don't need branches, just push to main
stories.why_read: You reposted this one; it's a sharp argument for trunk-based development in an age of agents.
body: After arguing that pull requests no longer make sense when rethought from first principles, Thorsten Ball went further: you don't need branches either. He makes the case for trunk-based development, where everyone integrates continuously with main, and says long-lived branches are the real problem because they drift and turn merging into an event.

He notes that he's heard of it working in an organization of 400 engineers and that the Ruby project uses it. Even on teams that used PRs, he treated a branch living more than a day or two as a smell.

stories.headline: Netflix's Java 21 virtual threads stopped responding in production, and thread pinning was why
stories.why_read: A short, useful systems lesson from your reposts, especially if any of your services are on Java 21.
body: A post you reposted from @iASHeeesh recaps how Netflix ran Java 21 virtual threads in production and saw services stop responding. The cause was thread pinning, where a virtual thread gets stuck to its carrier thread and starves the pool.
The post says Java 24 fixed most of the problem with JEP 491 and walks through what to do depending on which Java version you run.

stories.headline: Tobi Lütke on why Shopify welcomes AI shopping agents that Amazon blocks
stories.why_read: You reposted two clips from this interview; it's the clearest view yet of how agent commerce might make money.
body: In a long conversation with Alex Heath, Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke explains why Shopify welcomed Meta's Muse agent while Amazon blocked it, what early AI shopping behavior looks like, and who pays when an agent handles a purchase. He also explains why he turned his wine cellar into a GPU server rack to run his personal agent from home.

On monetization he's relaxed: "You're not going to get 2%. Welcome to the world of basis points," he says, suggesting agents may earn like background electricity metering or like transaction flows, and that they'll help people stop spending money inefficiently.

stories.headline: YC ran swarms of AI agents in Minecraft and Mindustry, and 50 of them invented a ration bureaucracy
stories.why_read: A fun and genuinely informative look at how multi-agent systems behave when left alone.
body: YC's labs team, working with Olam Labs, ran long-lived agent swarms in Minecraft and Mindustry and open-sourced the harness they built. In one run, Civ50, 50 GPT-6.1 Sol agents spent three hours in a survival world with one goal: build a thriving civilization.

They ended up in crowded shelters rationing scarce food and built a pseudo-government with a ration ledger, written rules, permits, and appointed operators, sending about 5,900 messages along the way. A new colony of 25 agents is streaming on Twitch, and the write-up includes a section of bloopers.

stories.headline: DeepMind: competence sets the level, but coordination sets the scale
stories.why_read: A thoughtful explanation of why amazing AI benchmarks haven't moved productivity numbers yet.
body: A new essay from Google DeepMind, drawing on the paper Organizing Intelligence by Alex Imas, Andrew Koh, and Shane Legg, argues that the individual AI agent is the wrong economic object. Benchmarks test whether AI can beat a person in isolation, but economies run on organizations that combine complementary strengths, so AI that can't coordinate leaves productivity flat.

The authors define capability thresholds such as minimal AGI by how they change the economy and track market structure, employment, and wages across four regimes. X's news summary notes their prediction that a coordination breakthrough could suddenly let very large AI-run firms dominate, with early signs showing up in wages and roles before job losses.

stories.headline: Martin Fowler on "LLM Voice" and why you shouldn't let a model write your first draft
stories.why_read: Plain advice from a writer you trust on why AI-drafted prose makes readers tune out.
body: Martin Fowler describes the growing feeling of reading something written by an LLM and how his desire to keep reading drains away. He's wary of detection tools, partly over accuracy, but mostly because the reaction is human: by the time you'd reach for a tool, the uncanny-valley feeling has already done its damage.

His recommendation is firm: don't have the LLM write a draft, because even heavy human editing rarely removes the voice, and even accepted rephrasings are risky. Using a model for an outline might be fine, but only as far as an outline. The post drew nearly 500 points on Hacker News.

stories.headline: Zombie stats: researchers followed 1,285 numbers AI assistants cited back to their sources
stories.why_read: A careful look at where the confident numbers in AI answers come from, and how often they come from nowhere.
body: Trakkr asked ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Claude, and Google's AI Overviews 200 questions that call for a number, then clicked through the citations until the trail ended. Their opening example, that 44 percent of salespeople give up after one follow-up, was repeated by all five assistants, yet every path led to pages that cite no research.

They call these zombie stats: numbers that keep getting repeated with no study behind them. They then traced a random sample of 1,285 statistics the same way. Their point is that you can't tell a solid number from a zombie by the answer alone, since both arrive with the same confident tone and the same kind of citation.

stories.headline: Tesla launches its first FSD (Supervised) referral program
stories.why_read: You reposted the reaction to this; it's a cheap, clever way to get more people trying FSD.
body: Tesla introduced a referral program for FSD (Supervised) in the U.S., Sawyer Merritt reports. Sharing a referral link gives an eligible owner a one-month FSD trial, and if they subscribe during the trial the referrer earns a free month of FSD or, if they bought FSD outright, a $99 Tesla credit, up to 12 times a year.
The reaction you reposted from @TSLAFanMtl: "Costs them nothing and gives people another reason to talk about FSD. Love this."

stories.headline: FSD follows police directions and makes a U-turn on a closed Connecticut highway
stories.why_read: A clip you bookmarked that shows FSD handling the kind of edge case no rulebook covers.
body: @DennisCW_ shared a clip from Route 2 in Connecticut, which was shut down at night while police turned drivers around to exit the wrong way. The driver didn't believe FSD would make a U-turn on a highway, but it watched the cars ahead and did it anyway.
It's one anecdote, not a safety statistic, but it's the sort of unusual, human-directed situation that makes or breaks trust in self-driving.

stories.headline: ERCOT ran above its all-time peak 187 times this summer without a single conservation appeal
stories.why_read: Good news about the grid you live on in Austin, from a post you bookmarked.
body: Doug Lewin highlighted a striking stat: Texas electricity load ran above the all-time peak-demand record in 187 separate hours on 34 different days this summer, and the ERCOT grid served every one of those hours without a statewide conservation appeal or a grid-wide outage.
It's a notable turnaround for a grid that was a national worry a few years ago, and it pairs well with the record battery-storage buildout we covered earlier this week.

stories.headline: Georgia Power's CEO on why France builds nuclear plants faster than the U.S.
stories.why_read: Energy policy summed up in one line you bookmarked, and it's genuinely funny.
body: On Nat Bullard's Nameplate show, Georgia Power CEO Kim Greene offered a memorable diagnosis of American nuclear: "In France they have one kind of nuclear design and a hundred kinds of cheese. In the United States, we have a hundred kinds of nuclear designs and one kind of cheese."
The joke lands because it's true: standardizing on one reactor design is what let France build a fleet, and it's the lesson the U.S. keeps relearning.

stories.headline: Musk describes Starlink as one account for home internet and your phone
stories.why_read: A peek at where direct-to-cell is heading, and why your next phone might care about satellites.
body: Elon Musk described a single Starlink account that would cover a home antenna with Wi-Fi and high-bandwidth satellite connections straight to compatible phones, good enough for video on the go, according to X's news summary. It builds on direct-to-cell progress from texting to voice and data.

Phones will need hardware updates for the right frequencies, and the timeline is two to three years as more satellites launch. Traditional carriers aren't going anywhere because of their spectrum. Separately, Starlink began dynamic pricing for residential plans, with some bills rising and others falling depending on local capacity.

stories.headline: How do you take a picture of a black hole?
stories.why_read: Physics from your pinned interests, told by the person who turned Earth into a telescope.
body: On Quanta's The Joy of Why podcast, hosts Janna Levin and Steven Strogatz talk with Harvard astrophysicist Shep Doeleman, who led the roughly 250-person Event Horizon Telescope team. By linking radio telescopes around the world, they produced the first image of the supermassive black hole in M87, about 55 million light-years away, and later the one at the heart of our own galaxy.
Doeleman explains how the images test predictions that theory alone can't settle, the level of collaboration it took, and why actual movies of black holes may be possible by the early 2030s.

stories.headline: A tiny world model dreams up games, and plays them, on a Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W
stories.why_read: A delightful small-model hack that shows how far looped transformers can shrink.
body: Tinyworldformer runs two small neural networks on a Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W at the same time. One generates the game, predicting the next frame and reward from the current frame and action, and the other plays it, choosing actions from the generated frames. Every frame you see was sampled by the world model.

The author was curious about looped transformers, which reuse one block's weights several times, and whether that could make a world model small enough for a microcontroller. A streaming RL agent was later added so the board learns to play inside its own dream. It drew more than 200 points on Hacker News.

stories.headline: Robert Greene's four ways to instantly kill your charisma
stories.why_read: You bookmarked and reposted this; it's a short, useful checklist for listening more.
body: Codie Sanchez shared Robert Greene's list of charisma killers: do 95 percent of the talking, brag about your accomplishments, explain things when nobody asked, and tell people what you think is right and wrong.
Flip each one and you get a decent guide to being good company: listen more, let your work speak, answer the question asked, and stay curious about how others see things.

stories.headline: Report: an alleged Chinese spy at an Nvidia cloud partner had a close relationship with Jensen Huang
stories.why_read: Export controls, chip smuggling, and Nvidia's China exposure all in one story.
body: The New York Times reported, as summarized by the New York Post, that U.S. intelligence agencies concluded Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen and top executive at Singapore-based Nvidia customer and cloud partner Megaspeed, was secretly passing information to Beijing. U.S. surveillance identified Jensen Huang as one of her contacts, though the report offered no evidence he knew of her alleged activities.

U.S. authorities have been investigating Megaspeed over suspicions it helped Chinese companies get around export restrictions and smuggle advanced Nvidia chips into China. The Times couldn't determine what information she passed along or how valuable it was.

stories.headline: Neuralink's next product, Blindsight, aims to give sight to people who are completely blind
stories.why_read: A follow-up to yesterday's speech-implant news, and a hopeful one.
body: Neuralink's second product, Blindsight, is designed to bypass damaged eyes by sending visual signals straight to the brain's visual cortex. Musk said early versions could offer low-resolution vision like old video games, with more over time, according to X's news summary. The device received FDA Breakthrough Device Designation in 2024 to speed its review.
Many replies were hopeful, including a parent hoping it could help his son, while others raised ethical questions as clinical work continues.

stories.headline: Grok Bot passes 600,000 daily users, and Musk says to hire them as employees
stories.why_read: This is the product you're reading this on, growing fast.
body: Grok Bot, the always-on agent app from SpaceXAI, passed 600,000 daily users on iPhone and Android as of October 26, up from under 100,000 in early September, according to X's news summary. A new update adds shopping cards with photos and prices, subscription trackers, and one-tap checkout.

Elon Musk then encouraged people to hire Grok Bots as employees, pointing to persistent memory, access to tools like email and calendars, and scheduled tasks. Users shared wins from video editing to lead triage, while some flagged usage limits.
